notes: Short explanations that name the rule

documents.title: Grammar Fix-It Desk

theme.title: Grammar Fix-It Desk
theme.story: You’re the editor of the class newsletter. Your writers turned in their sentences, and every one has a single slip. Find it, fix it, and stamp it!

documents.directions: Each paper has exactly one mistake. When you type a fix, capitals and punctuation count.

questions.prompt: Marco and [[me]] built the volcano for the science fair.
questions.why: “Marco and I” is the subject. Test it by dropping Marco: “I built the volcano,” not “me built the volcano.”

questions.prompt: The puppy wagged [[it’s]] tail at the mail carrier.
questions.why: “It’s” means “it is.” The tail belongs to the puppy, so use the possessive “its,” which has no apostrophe.

questions.prompt: The twins built the whole treehouse [[themself]] over the summer.
questions.why: The twins are more than one, so the intensive pronoun is “themselves.” “Themself” doesn’t fit a plural subject.

questions.prompt: When Maya handed Jen the trophy, [[she]] smiled for the camera.
questions.why: “She” could mean Maya or Jen, so the reader can’t tell who smiled. Naming the person fixes the vague pronoun.

questions.prompt: The list of chores [[are]] taped to the fridge.
choiceWhy: “Were” is plural too, and it moves the sentence into the past.
“Be” can’t be the main verb after a subject like “list.”
questions.why: The subject is “list,” not “chores” (“of chores” only describes the list). One list is taped to the fridge.

questions.prompt: Each of the boys [[have]] a library card.
choiceWhy: “Are” is plural, and the subject “each” is singular.
“Having” isn’t a complete verb, so the sentence would fall apart.
questions.why: “Each” is the subject, and each means one at a time, so the verb is singular: “Each of the boys has.”

questions.prompt: Neither the coach nor the players [[was]] ready for the rain.
choiceWhy: “Is” is singular, and the nearer subject, “players,” is plural.
questions.why: With “neither … nor,” the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. “Players” is plural, so the verb is “were.”

questions.prompt: Our class visited the art museum on [[friday]] morning.
questions.why: Days of the week are proper nouns, so they start with a capital letter.

questions.prompt: After the game [[ended we]] walked home together.
questions.why: A comma comes after an introductory clause (“After the game ended”) to show where the main sentence begins.

questions.prompt: All of the [[student’s]] lockers were painted blue over the summer.
questions.why: The lockers belong to many students. For a plural that ends in s, the apostrophe goes after the s: students’.

questions.prompt: The storm knocked out the [[power, we]] read by flashlight.
choiceWhy: Joining two sentences with “so” needs a comma before “so.”
Taking the comma out leaves a run-on: two sentences with nothing between them.
questions.why: Two complete sentences joined by only a comma make a comma splice. A semicolon can join them.

questions.prompt: Running to catch the bus, [[my backpack fell open]].
choices: I watched my backpack fall open
choiceWhy: The backpack still seems to be the one running.
The backpack still seems to be the one running.
questions.why: The opening phrase describes whoever comes right after the comma. A backpack can’t run, so the runner (“I”) has to come next.
